findings.issue_text: The credential-sync branch in refreshOAuthTokens returns a native Response instead of the provider-specific token/Axios response shapes expected by Google, HubSpot, and Zoho, causing refresh failures when sharing is enabled
Google Calendar persists the Zod safeParse wrapper {success, data} instead of the parsed token object, corrupting credentials after the first refresh when sharing is disabled

parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed schema keys that stringify to the same property name, overwriting the numeric requirement and stripping expiry and provider-specific fields from synchronized tokens

Credential-sync requests include only an enumerable user ID and public app slug with no secret or authorization header, so the endpoint cannot authenticate token-fetch requests without out-of-band controls
Zoho Bigin passes credentialId to refreshOAuthTokens where a user ID is required, potentially fetching another user's token on ID collision or causing refresh failure
Salesforce bypasses refreshOAuthTokens and refreshes directly with Salesforce, ignoring the configured credential-sync endpoint and potentially diverging from authoritative parent credentials

The app-credential webhook identifies credentials only by userId and appId and updates an unordered findFirst result, so users with multiple accounts for one app can have an arbitrary credential overwritten
The webhook's findFirst-then-create sequence is non-atomic, allowing concurrent or retried deliveries to create duplicate credential rows

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Credential-sync requests include only an enumerable user ID and public app slug with no secret or authorization header, so the endpoint cannot authenticate token-fetch requests without out-of-band controls

adjudication.rationale: Looking at refreshOAuthTokens.ts, when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true, it makes a POST request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT with only calcomUserId and appSlug in the body. There is no authentication header or secret included in this outbound request. This is a legitimate security concern - the external credential sync endpoint has no way to verify that requests are coming from a legitimate Cal.com instance. The webhook endpoint (app-credential.ts) does verify incoming requests with CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, but the outbound requests from refreshOAuthTokens have no authentication mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The app-credential webhook identifies credentials only by userId and appId and updates an unordered findFirst result, so users with multiple accounts for one app can have an arbitrary credential overwritten

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the webhook handler in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts, the code uses `prisma.credential.findFirst` with only `userId` and `appId` as filters (lines 57-64). If a user has multiple credentials for the same app (e.g., multiple Google Calendar accounts), findFirst returns an arbitrary one without any ordering specified. The code then either updates this arbitrary credential or creates a new one. This is a real correctness issue - when syncing credentials for a user with multiple accounts of the same app type, the wrong credential could be updated, potentially corrupting the user's integration setup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The webhook's findFirst-then-create sequence is non-atomic, allowing concurrent or retried deliveries to create duplicate credential rows

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the webhook handler in apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts, the code does a findFirst to check if a credential exists (lines 56-64), then either updates or creates based on the result (lines 66-85). This is indeed a non-atomic read-then-write pattern. If two concurrent webhook deliveries arrive for the same userId/appId combination, both could execute findFirst before either executes create, resulting in duplicate credential rows. This is a real race condition that could cause data integrity issues.
